intro.en: Core surgical tubes, urinary catheters, enteral feeding lines, thoracic drains, airway devices, vascular catheters, and wound drainage systems tested as spotters in the MBBS practical examination.

items.summary: A flexible latex or silicone urinary catheter with an inflatable retention balloon and two channels, used for continuous bladder drainage.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Flexible tubular catheter with a smooth rounded tip and two subterminal drainage eyes.
Features a proximal Y-junction with two ports: a straight drainage funnel and a side inflation arm with a one-way colour-coded valve.
Inflation valve is stamped with French gauge size (e.g., 14 Fr to 18 Fr) and balloon volume (usually 5 to 10 mL).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Continuous bladder drainage and hourly urinary output monitoring in shock, major trauma, and sepsis.
Relieving acute or chronic urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia or urethral stricture.
Decompressing the urinary bladder before and during pelvic and lower abdominal surgery.
Managing neurogenic bladder and immobility.

blocks.title: Steps of insertion
bullets: Maintain strict aseptic precautions; clean the urethral meatus with antiseptic.
Instill 10 mL of 2% lignocaine jelly into the urethra and wait 3 to 5 minutes.
Gently advance the catheter until urine emerges into the drainage channel.
In males, advance fully up to the Y-bifurcation to ensure the balloon is completely within the bladder.
Inflate balloon with 10 mL sterile water (never normal saline or air), then withdraw gently until seated at the bladder neck.
Connect the drainage port to a sterile closed urinary drainage bag.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI).
Urethral trauma and false passage formation if inflated within the prostate or spongy urethra.
Catheter encrustation and luminal blockage by struvite crystals.
Urethral stricture from prolonged catheterisation or pressure necrosis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Inflate only with sterile water: saline crystallizes and blocks the inflation channel; air allows the balloon to float away from the bladder neck.
French gauge (Charriere): circumference in millimetres (1 Fr = 1/3 mm external diameter; 18 Fr = 6 mm diameter).

viva.q: Why must sterile water be used to inflate the retention balloon instead of saline?
viva.a: Saline crystals can deposit within the microscopic inflation channel, jamming the valve and preventing balloon deflation during removal.

viva.q: What does the French (Charriere) gauge indicate?
viva.a: It measures the external circumference in millimetres; external diameter equals French size divided by 3 (1 Fr = 0.33 mm).

viva.q: What essential clinical step confirms safe intravesical placement before balloon inflation in men?
viva.a: Advancing the catheter all the way to the Y-bifurcation after urine flows ensures the balloon is not inflated inside the urethra.

image.brief: Latex two-way Foley catheter displaying the inflated spherical balloon at the tip and proximal dual-channel Y-bifurcation.

items.summary: A large-bore silicone or latex catheter with three independent lumens engineered for continuous post-operative bladder irrigation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy-calibre catheter (typically 20 Fr to 24 Fr) with three separate proximal ports.
Port 1: side valve for inflating the heavy retention balloon (30 to 50 mL capacity).
Port 2: wide central channel for evacuation of urine, irrigation fluid, and blood clots.
Port 3: narrow infusion channel with a luer lock for connecting continuous irrigation fluid bags.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Continuous bladder irrigation following transurethral resection of prostate (TURP) or open prostatectomy.
Management of severe gross haematuria with clot retention following transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT).
Achieving mechanical balloon tamponade of the prostatic venous plexus using a large 30 to 50 mL balloon.

blocks.title: Mechanism and complications
bullets: Continuous influx of isotonic normal saline flushes out bleeding before intravesical blood clots can form and obstruct the outlet.
Complications include clot retention if outflow is blocked, severe bladder distension, and TURP syndrome from excessive glycine absorption.

viva.q: What are the three specific lumens of a three-way Foley catheter?
viva.a: A balloon inflation lumen, an inflow lumen for irrigating fluid, and a large-bore outflow lumen for urine, irrigant, and blood clots.

viva.q: Why is continuous irrigation necessary following prostate resection?
viva.a: To flush fresh bleeding out of the bladder constantly, preventing blood clots from organizing and obstructing the catheter.

viva.q: What fluid is used for continuous postoperative bladder irrigation on the ward?
viva.a: Sterile normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride) is used once the operative procedure is completed.

image.brief: Three-way Foley catheter displaying its three distinct proximal hubs, large drainage channel, and distended 30 mL balloon.

items.summary: A red rubber or silicone catheter with expandable bat-wing flanges at the tip used for suprapubic cystostomy, gastrostomy, or nephrostomy.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Semi-rigid red rubber or clear silicone tube with a single wide drainage lumen.
Distal end features 2 or 4 expandable outward-flaring wings (bat-wings) that form a self-retaining basket.
Lacks an inflatable balloon; proximal end is a wide funnel.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Open suprapubic cystostomy (SPC) for urinary diversion in urethral disruption or complex stricture.
Open tube gastrostomy or feeding enterostomy in esophageal obstruction.
Nephrostomy drainage following open stone surgery.
Tube cecostomy or tube cholecystostomy in unfit emergency patients.

blocks.title: Technique of insertion and removal
bullets: Insertion: a rigid metallic introducer is passed down the lumen to stretch the tip, flattening the wings into a straight tube.
Once inside the viscera, the introducer is withdrawn, allowing the wings to spring open and lock.
Removal: requires firm steady traction or re-straightening with an introducer; prolonged placement causes encrustation around the wings.

viva.q: How does a Malecot catheter maintain self-retention without an inflatable balloon?
viva.a: The preformed elastic wings at the tip spring open inside the hollow organ, mechanically anchoring it against the wall.

viva.q: How is the Malecot catheter straightened during operative insertion?
viva.a: A rigid metal introducer is passed through the lumen to pull and stretch the tip, collapsing the wings flat along the shaft.

viva.q: Name two non-urological surgical uses of a Malecot catheter.
viva.a: Open feeding tube gastrostomy and tube cecostomy or emergency cholecystostomy.

image.brief: Red rubber Malecot catheter showing the four expandable bat-wings open at the distal tip and the wide funnel hub at the base.

items.summary: A single-lumen vulcanized red rubber catheter with a solid rounded tip and lateral eye, used for intermittent bladder evacuation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Semi-rigid opaque orange or red vulcanized rubber tube with a single drainage lumen.
Smooth rounded closed tip with a single lateral drainage eye.
Proximal end is a plain tapered funnel without balloons or side ports.
Non-self-retaining; slips out unless taped or manually held.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Intermittent clean bladder catheterisation.
Decompressing the bladder immediately prior to minor pelvic surgery or obstetric delivery.
Measuring true post-void residual urine volume.
Collecting an uncontaminated sterile urine specimen for culture.

blocks.title: Non-urological uses
bullets: Posterior nasal packing for intractable epistaxis.
Emergency digital tourniquet during surgery on fingers and toes.
Tourniquet around the base of the penis during circumcision or hypospadias repair.
Rectal flatus tube to decompress gaseous abdominal distension.

viva.q: How does a Nelaton straight catheter differ from a Foley catheter?
viva.a: Nelaton is a single-lumen, non-retaining tube without a balloon, used for one-time intermittent drainage.

viva.q: What is considered normal post-void residual urine volume in an adult?
viva.a: Less than 50 mL is considered normal; residual volume exceeding 100 mL indicates significant outflow obstruction or detrusor failure.

viva.q: Name two emergency non-urological surgical uses of a red rubber catheter.
viva.a: Controlling posterior nasal epistaxis as a pack, and serving as a temporary digital tourniquet in finger surgery.

image.brief: Straight single-lumen red rubber Nelaton catheter displaying its rounded solid tip, lateral eye, and simple funnel hub.

items.summary: A sharp curved trocar and cannula set designed for percutaneous suprapubic puncture and catheterisation of a distended urinary bladder.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy curved metallic or plastic trocar with a sharp triangular cutting point.
Surrounded by a peel-away split sheath cannula or sliding sleeve.
Supplied with an appropriately sized Foley or Malecot catheter and fixation collar.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Emergency relief of acute urinary retention when urethral catheterisation fails (urethral stricture, acute prostatitis, pelvic fracture).
Traumatic urethral disruption with pelvic hematoma.
Long-term urinary diversion in paraplegic patients to avoid urethral erosion.

blocks.title: Prerequisites and insertion steps
bullets: Absolute prerequisite: the urinary bladder must be clinically palpable and dull to percussion above the pubic symphysis.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic 2 cm above the pubic symphysis in the midline.
Confirm bladder entry by exploratory syringe aspiration of clear urine.
Introduce trocar and cannula pointing slightly downwards into the pelvis; withdraw trocar.
Pass catheter through cannula into the bladder, inflate balloon, and peel away or withdraw cannula.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Small bowel perforation if the bladder was insufficiently distended and overlying peritoneum was transgressed.
Prevesical haematoma in the cave of Retzius; haematuria; pericatheter urine leak.

viva.q: What absolute physical finding must be confirmed before percutaneous suprapubic puncture?
viva.a: The bladder must be palpably distended and dull to percussion above the pubic symphysis, ensuring the peritoneal reflection is displaced upwards.

viva.q: What is the anatomical landmark for percutaneous suprapubic cystostomy?
viva.a: In the midline, approximately two finger-breadths (2 cm) superior to the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

viva.q: Why is suprapubic catheterisation indicated in acute pelvic fracture with blood at the urethral meatus?
viva.a: Blind urethral catheterisation can convert a partial urethral tear into a complete transection and introduce infection into the pelvic haematoma.

image.brief: Curved metallic suprapubic cystostomy trocar and split sheath cannula shown with a matching balloon catheter on a sterile drape.

items.summary: A flexible radio-opaque PVC tube with lead-shot weighted tip and depth rings used for gastric decompression and enteral nutrition.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Transparent PVC or rubber tube with a continuous radio-opaque line along its length.
Features 4 circular black depth rings printed at 40 cm, 50 cm, 60 cm, and 70 cm from the tip.
Distal end contains small lead beads (radio-opaque pellets) and 4 staggered side drainage eyes.
Proximal end has a funnel connector with an attached plug.

blocks.title: Anatomical distance markings
bullets: 40 cm ring: corresponds to the cardiac orifice (gastro-esophageal junction).
50 cm ring: corresponds to the body of the stomach.
60 cm ring: reaches the pylorus.
70 cm ring: enters the second part of the duodenum.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Gastric decompression in acute mechanical intestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, and acute peritonitis.
Enteral feeding in unconscious or dysphagic patients.
Gastric lavage in acute poisoning and drug overdose.
Diagnostic gastric aspirate for blood in upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

blocks.title: Verifying correct tube position
bullets: Auscultation test: auscultate epigastrium with stethoscope while injecting 20 mL of air, hearing a loud gurgle or whoosh.
Aspiration test: aspirate fluid and check pH with litmus paper; pH below 5.5 confirms acidic gastric contents.
Gold standard: chest radiograph showing the radio-opaque line descending below the left diaphragm.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Accidental bronchial or tracheal intubation leading to fatal chemical aspiration pneumonia.
Alar cartilage pressure necrosis and ulceration of the nostril.
Esophageal erosions, strictures, and metabolic hypochloremic alkalosis from excessive aspiration.

viva.q: What do the four depth markings on a Ryles tube signify?
viva.a: 40 cm reaches the cardiac orifice, 50 cm reaches the body of the stomach, 60 cm reaches the pylorus, and 70 cm reaches the duodenum.

viva.q: What is the gold standard method to verify correct nasogastric tube position?
viva.a: A chest and upper abdominal radiograph demonstrating the radio-opaque tip below the left hemi-diaphragm inside the stomach.

viva.q: Why does the distal tip contain lead pellets?
viva.a: The weighted tip uses gravity to guide the tube along the posterior pharyngeal wall into the esophagus during swallowing.

image.brief: Clear PVC Ryles nasogastric tube displaying lead pellets in the tip, radio-opaque line, and graduated black ring markings.

items.summary: A triple-lumen tube with an esophageal balloon and a gastric balloon used for emergency mechanical tamponade of bleeding varices.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy red rubber or silicone tube equipped with three proximal ports and two inflatable balloons.
Balloons: a spherical distal gastric balloon and a long cylindrical proximal esophageal balloon.
Ports: gastric aspiration lumen (large central hub), gastric balloon inflation port, and esophageal balloon inflation port.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Emergency control of massive variceal haemorrhage in portal hypertension when endoscopic band ligation fails or is unavailable.
Temporary life-saving bridge to definitive endoscopic therapy, TIPS, or surgery.

blocks.title: Steps of insertion and inflation
bullets: Check balloon integrity and airtightness by submerging under water before passing.
Intubate trachea beforehand in drowsy patients to protect airway against aspiration.
Lubricate tube and pass through mouth or nose into the stomach.
Inflate gastric balloon with 250 mL of air (or 50 mL dilute contrast); clamp inflation channel.
Gently withdraw tube until resistance is felt as the gastric balloon snugs against the gastro-esophageal junction.
Maintain gentle continuous traction (0.5 to 1.0 kg) using a sponge or pulley system.
If bleeding persists, inflate the esophageal balloon to 30 to 45 mmHg using a manometer.

blocks.title: Complications and precautions
bullets: Esophageal rupture if the gastric balloon is accidentally inflated inside the esophagus.
Asphyxiation: if the gastric balloon ruptures or slips into the pharynx, the esophageal balloon occludes the larynx.
Crucial precaution: a pair of scissors must be kept taped to the head of the bed to immediately transect all lumens if airway obstruction occurs.
Mucosal necrosis: esophageal balloon must be deflated for 10 minutes every 3 to 4 hours to preserve mucosal perfusion.

viva.q: What are the three lumens of the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube?
viva.a: Gastric aspiration lumen, gastric balloon inflation lumen, and esophageal balloon inflation lumen.

viva.q: Why must a pair of scissors always be kept at the bedside?
viva.a: If the balloon migrates upwards into the pharynx and obstructs the airway, cutting all three lumens instantly deflates both balloons.

viva.q: How does the Minnesota tube differ from the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube?
viva.a: The Minnesota tube has a fourth lumen dedicated to continuous esophageal aspiration above the balloon, preventing saliva aspiration.

image.brief: Sengstaken-Blakemore tube with inflated spherical gastric balloon, elongated esophageal balloon, and triple-port proximal hub.

items.summary: A four-lumen gastroesophageal balloon tamponade tube with dedicated esophageal suction to prevent pulmonary aspiration.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Modified balloon tamponade tube featuring four labeled proximal extension lines.
Channels: gastric balloon inflation, esophageal balloon inflation, gastric aspiration, and esophageal aspiration.
Features multiple side suction holes above the esophageal balloon for salivary drainage.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Emergency balloon tamponade of exsanguinating gastroesophageal varices in cirrhotic portal hypertension.
Superior to the Sengstaken tube because continuous esophageal suction prevents pooling and pulmonary aspiration of oral secretions.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Esophageal balloon pressure is monitored with a sphygmomanometer and kept strictly between 30 and 45 mmHg.
Tamponade should not exceed 24 hours total duration to prevent ischemic esophageal ulceration and perforation.

viva.q: What is the crucial advantage of the Minnesota tube over the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube?
viva.a: A fourth lumen provides continuous aspiration of esophageal secretions proximal to the balloon, preventing pulmonary aspiration.

viva.q: Name all four lumens of the Minnesota tube.
viva.a: Gastric balloon inflation, esophageal balloon inflation, gastric aspiration, and esophageal aspiration.

viva.q: What is the maximum duration balloon tamponade can be safely maintained?
viva.a: Not more than 24 hours total, with periodic deflation of the esophageal balloon every 3 to 4 hours to avoid necrosis.

image.brief: Minnesota four-lumen tube showing its four distinct labeled ports, inflated gastric and esophageal balloons, and suction eyes.

items.summary: A flexible T-shaped rubber or silicone tube placed into the common bile duct after choledochotomy to provide biliary drainage.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: T-shaped tube made of amber vulcanized rubber or clear silicone.
Composed of two short horizontal limbs that sit inside the common bile duct (CBD) and a long vertical stem that exits the abdominal wall.
Available in French calibres 12 Fr to 18 Fr.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Decompressing the common bile duct and preventing bile leak after choledochotomy and open exploration.
Splinting the common bile duct during primary repair or duct reconstruction.
Providing a conduit for postoperative T-tube cholangiography to detect retained biliary stones.

blocks.title: Steps of insertion and trimming
bullets: The horizontal limbs are trimmed short (2 to 3 cm) and notched or guttered longitudinally on the posterior wall.
Notching allows the limbs to fold together like a single stem during removal.
Inserted into the choledochotomy; duct closed snugly around vertical stem with 4-0 absorbable sutures.
Brought out through a separate stab incision in the right hypochondrium; connected to a sterile gravity bile bag.

blocks.title: Postoperative management and removal
bullets: Normal daily bile drainage is 400 to 800 mL; colour transitions from dark green to golden yellow.
Postoperative T-tube cholangiogram is performed on day 7 to 10 to confirm free flow into duodenum and absence of stones.
If cholangiogram is normal, the tube is clamped for 24 hours: if no pain, fever, or jaundice develops, it is ready for removal.
Removed at 14 to 21 days: this allows a dense, mature fibrous tract to form around the stem, preventing intraperitoneal bile peritonitis.

viva.q: Why is a Kehr T-tube left in place for at least 14 to 21 days before extraction?
viva.a: To allow a mature, watertight fibrous track to form around the stem, ensuring bile does not leak into the peritoneal cavity upon removal.

viva.q: What investigation must be performed before removing a T-tube?
viva.a: A T-tube cholangiogram on postoperative day 7 to 10 to demonstrate free contrast flow into the duodenum and exclude retained stones.

viva.q: Why are the horizontal limbs of the T-tube notched longitudinally before insertion?
viva.a: Notching allows the horizontal limbs to collapse and fold alongside each other, enabling smooth extraction through the ductotomy.

image.brief: Amber rubber Kehr T-tube showing the notched horizontal crossbar and the long vertical drainage stem on a sterile tray.

items.summary: A fine-bore flexible PVC tube with two lateral eyes and a colour-coded female luer mount used for paediatric enteral feeding.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Slender, soft, clear PVC tube (typically 40 to 100 cm long) graduated in centimetres.
Smooth rounded closed tip with two staggered lateral eyes.
Proximal end has a female luer-lock hub with a colour-coded plug (5 Fr grey, 6 Fr light green, 7 Fr orange, 8 Fr blue, 10 Fr black).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Enteral nutrition and gastric decompression in neonates, premature infants, and paediatric patients.
Diagnostic sounding of esophageal atresia or choanal atresia in a newborn at birth.
Catheterising urinary stomas, suprapubic buttons, and ureteric splints.
Administering local anaesthetic wound infusions for post-operative analgesia.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: In adults requiring long-term nasogastric feeding, small-bore tubes produce far less nasal ulceration and reflux than Ryles tubes.
Confirm position by aspirating acidic stomach juice before instilling any milk or feeds.

viva.q: How is congenital esophageal atresia excluded at birth using an infant feeding tube?
viva.a: A stiff 10 Fr feeding tube passed through the mouth will arrest at 10 to 12 cm from the alveolar margin if atresia is present.

viva.q: Why is an infant feeding tube preferred over a standard Ryles tube for prolonged enteral feeding in adults?
viva.a: Its narrow calibre and supple plastic drastically reduce alar pressure necrosis, pharyngeal irritation, and gastroesophageal reflux.

viva.q: What do the colour-coded proximal plugs signify on infant feeding tubes?
viva.a: They designate the French gauge diameter (e.g., 5 Fr grey, 6 Fr green, 8 Fr blue, 10 Fr black).

image.brief: Fine-gauge infant feeding tube coiled on a sterile cloth showing centimetre depth markings and blue 8 Fr luer hub with cap.

items.summary: A flat sheet of vulcanized rubber with parallel longitudinal corrugations designed to drain superficial wound collections by capillary action.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Flat ribbon of flexible orange, amber, or red vulcanized rubber.
Features alternating parallel longitudinal grooves and ridges (corrugations) on both sides.
Can be cut longitudinally or transversely to suit wound dimensions.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Draining superficial subcutaneous wound collections.
Draining ischiorectal or perianal abscess cavities after deroofing.
Scrotal haematoma drainage and superficial groin wounds.
Draining the thyroid bed after open thyroid surgery.

blocks.title: Mechanism and management
bullets: Functions as a passive open drain; fluid travels along the grooves by surface tension and capillary action into the absorbent outer dressing.
Secured to the wound edge with a non-absorbable silk suture; a sterile safety pin is placed through the outer end to prevent inward migration.
Shortened by 1 to 2 cm daily and removed completely by 48 to 72 hours.
Major drawback: open pathway allows retrograde colonization of skin bacteria into the wound.

viva.q: By what physical mechanism does a corrugated rubber drain evacuate wound fluid?
viva.a: Capillary action along the corrugated channels and gravity drainage into the overlying sterile absorbent dressing.

viva.q: Why is a safety pin or anchoring suture passed through the exteriorised end?
viva.a: To prevent the loose flexible drain from being sucked inward or accidentally slipping into deep wound cavities.

viva.q: Why should a corrugated drain not be kept in place beyond 48 to 72 hours?
viva.a: It is an open drainage system that permits retrograde migration of pathogenic skin bacteria into the healing wound.

image.brief: Amber-coloured corrugated rubber drain sheet showing parallel longitudinal grooved channels and a safety pin through one margin.

items.summary: An active closed drainage system featuring a multi-perforated catheter connected to a compressible vacuum bellows or bulb to collapse dead space.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Perforated clear silicone or PVC tubing with multiple side holes and a radio-opaque marker stripe.
Connected via a one-way non-return valve to an active suction reservoir (accordion-like spring bellows or flexible silicone bulb).
The reservoir is compressed manually before sealing to generate negative suction pressure.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Draining extensive dead spaces following modified radical mastectomy and axillary clearance.
Neck dissection and total thyroidectomy.
Major orthopaedic joint replacement (total hip and total knee arthroplasty).
Pelvic lymphadenectomy and major soft tissue tumor resections.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Continuous negative suction evacuates blood and seroma, pulling skin flaps tightly against underlying muscle.
Closed airtight circuit prevents atmospheric exposure and halts retrograde bacterial infection.
Allows precise volumetric and visual measurement of daily drainage.

blocks.title: Criteria for removal
bullets: Removed when 24-hour collection drops below 20 to 30 mL of clear serous fluid (typically post-op day 2 to 5 depending on surgery).

viva.q: What are the two major advantages of active negative suction in mastectomy wounds?
viva.a: Continuous evacuation of blood and seroma prevents seroma formation, while suction adheres skin flaps to the chest wall.

viva.q: Why is a closed suction drain superior to an open corrugated drain?
viva.a: The sealed airtight system prevents atmospheric contamination, drastically lowering the risk of wound infection.

viva.q: What is the clinical criterion for removing a suction drain after breast surgery?
viva.a: When the 24-hour drain output decreases to less than 20 to 30 mL of serous fluid with no signs of active bleeding.

image.brief: Closed suction drain set showing multi-hole perforated silicone tube connected to a compressed transparent spring bellows.

items.summary: A firm silicone or PVC tube with multiple side perforations placed in dependent peritoneal recesses for gravity drainage of fluid collections.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Clear semi-rigid PVC or silicone tubing (usually 20 Fr to 32 Fr) with a continuous blue radio-opaque line.
Distal 5 to 10 cm possesses multiple oval or circular side perforations.
Connected to a sterile gravity drainage collection bag.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Placed in dependent abdominal recesses (Morison pouch, pouch of Douglas, subphrenic space) following peritonitis or trauma.
Drainage following perforated peptic ulcer repair, appendicular peritonitis, and pancreatic necrosectomy.
Monitoring for early anastomotic dehiscence or occult bile leak after gastrointestinal surgery.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Always brought out through a separate airtight stab wound rather than the main laparotomy incision.
Bringing it through the primary incision promotes wound breakdown, dehiscence, and incisional hernia.
Prolonged contact between a rigid tube and bowel can cause pressure necrosis and an enterocutaneous fistula.

viva.q: Why must an abdominal tube drain exit through a separate stab incision?
viva.a: Bringing the drain through the main wound invites wound infection, impairs fascial healing, and predisposes to incisional hernia.

viva.q: What anatomical spaces in the peritoneal cavity are chosen for dependent drain placement?
viva.a: The hepatorenal pouch of Morison in the upper abdomen and the pouch of Douglas in the pelvis.

viva.q: What complication can arise from keeping a rigid tube drain against bowel loops too long?
viva.a: Focal pressure necrosis of the intestinal wall, leading to bowel perforation and enterocutaneous fistula.

image.brief: Clear silicone abdominal tube drain showing multiple rounded side eyes, radio-opaque line, and drainage bag connector.

items.summary: A heavy semi-rigid PVC tube with a radio-opaque stripe and sentinel eye inserted into the pleural cavity to evacuate air, blood, or pus.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Thick-walled transparent plastic or silicone tube with numbered depth graduations in centimetres.
Continuous blue radio-opaque line that is interrupted at the most proximal side hole (sentinel eye).
Sizes: 16 Fr to 24 Fr for pneumothorax; 28 Fr to 36 Fr for haemothorax or thick empyema.
Distal end is open with a slight bevel.

blocks.title: Triangle of safety
bullets: Anatomical zone for safe chest tube insertion to avoid neurovascular and visceral injury.
Anterior boundary: lateral border of pectoralis major muscle.
Posterior boundary: anterior border of latissimus dorsi muscle.
Inferior boundary: horizontal line at the level of the 5th intercostal space (nipple level).
Apex: base of the axilla.

blocks.title: Steps of insertion
bullets: Infiltrate 1% lignocaine with adrenaline into skin, intercostal muscles, and parietal pleura.
Make a 2 cm transverse skin incision over the 5th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line.
Bluntly dissect with curved artery forceps immediately over the upper border of the lower rib to avoid the subcostal bundle.
Puncture parietal pleura with forceps; feel sudden loss of resistance or air rush; sweep finger inside to clear lung adhesions.
Insert clamped ICD tube: directed apically and anteriorly for pneumothorax, or postero-basally for fluid.
Verify all side eyes including the sentinel eye are inside the pleural cavity; connect to underwater seal.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intercostal vessel laceration causing massive haemothorax.
Lung parenchymal puncture; diaphragmatic, liver, or spleen laceration if placed too low.
Subcutaneous emphysema from misplaced side eye outside the ribs; re-expansion pulmonary oedema.

viva.q: What are the anatomical boundaries of the thoracic triangle of safety?
viva.a: Anterior: lateral border of pectoralis major; posterior: anterior border of latissimus dorsi; inferior: 5th intercostal space; apex: axillary floor.

viva.q: Why must the chest tube enter strictly over the superior border of the rib?
viva.a: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve travel along the subcostal groove on the inferior border of the rib.

viva.q: What is the clinical significance of the sentinel hole on an ICD tube?
viva.a: It is the most proximal fenestration; on a chest radiograph, this gap in the radio-opaque line must lie fully inside the pleural space.

image.brief: Heavy intercostal drainage catheter showing blue radio-opaque stripe interrupted at the sentinel eye, depth marks, and bevelled tip.

items.summary: An airtight collection system with a submerged tube creating a one-way hydraulic valve that allows pleural air and fluid to escape without re-entry.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Graduated transparent plastic or glass bottle with an airtight rubber cap.
Features two tubes: a long rigid tube submerged 2 to 3 cm below sterile water, and a short air vent open to the atmosphere.
The submerged tube connects via heavy flexible tubing to the patient intercostal drain.

blocks.title: Mechanism of function
bullets: Functions as a one-way water valve.
During expiration and coughing, positive pleural pressure drives air and fluid down the submerged tube, bubbling through water to escape via the vent.
During inspiration, negative intrapleural pressure draws water up the submerged tube, creating a hydrostatic column that prevents atmospheric air entering the chest.

blocks.title: Clinical observation and rules
bullets: Normal column swings (oscillates) 2 to 6 cm with respiratory cycles; proves patency of the tube.
Continuous bubbling signifies an active bronchopleural fistula or ongoing pneumothorax.
Cessation of swing indicates either full lung expansion or complete tube blockage by clot.
Must always remain at least 60 cm below the patient chest to prevent retrograde siphoning of fluid.
Never clamp the tube during transport: clamping in the presence of an air leak creates a lethal tension pneumothorax.

viva.q: Why is the long glass tube submerged exactly 2 to 3 cm below water?
viva.a: Submersion creates a one-way water seal: air easily escapes against 2 cm water resistance, while atmospheric air cannot be sucked into the pleura.

viva.q: What does swinging of the fluid column indicate?
viva.a: Swinging proves that the intercostal tube is patent and communicates freely with the pleural space experiencing respiratory pressure changes.

viva.q: Why should an underwater seal bottle never be lifted above chest level?
viva.a: Lifting the bottle above the chest reverses the hydrostatic gradient, allowing contaminated water to siphon directly into the pleural cavity.

image.brief: Clear graduated underwater seal bottle showing central tube submerged 2 cm below water line and short vent open to room air.

items.summary: A curved polyvinyl chloride tube with an inflatable low-pressure cuff, radio-opaque line, and Murphy eye used for mechanical ventilation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Curved clear PVC tube with centimetre depth markings printed along its shaft.
Features a universal 15 mm machine connector at the proximal end.
Equipped with a fine inflation line leading to a pilot balloon with a one-way spring valve.
Distal end has an inflatable cylindrical cuff and a side opening (Murphy eye) opposite the beveled tip.

blocks.title: Functions of key components
bullets: Low-pressure high-volume cuff seals the trachea, enabling positive-pressure ventilation and preventing gastric aspiration.
Murphy eye provides an alternate ventilation channel if the primary distal bevel impinges against the tracheal wall.
Radio-opaque line allows verification of tube tip position on chest radiograph.

blocks.title: Cuff pressure and sizing
bullets: Optimal cuff pressure is 20 to 30 cmH2O, measured with a cuff manometer.
Pressures above 30 cmH2O exceed capillary perfusion pressure, causing tracheal mucosal ischemia and late tracheal stenosis.
Pressures below 20 cmH2O permit silent microaspiration of pharyngeal secretions.
Adult female sizing: 7.0 to 7.5 mm internal diameter (depth 21 cm at incisors); adult male sizing: 8.0 to 8.5 mm (depth 23 cm).

viva.q: What is the function of the Murphy eye on an endotracheal tube?
viva.a: It acts as a safety bypass channel, maintaining gas flow if the primary terminal bevel becomes obstructed against the tracheal wall.

viva.q: What is the safe range for endotracheal cuff pressure and why?
viva.a: 20 to 30 cmH2O; higher pressures cause tracheal mucosal ischemia and stenosis, while lower pressures allow aspiration.

viva.q: What does the number printed on an endotracheal tube represent?
viva.a: It denotes the internal diameter (ID) of the tube lumen in millimetres.

image.brief: Cuffed polyvinyl chloride endotracheal tube displaying 15 mm machine adapter, pilot balloon, inflated clear cuff, and Murphy eye.

items.summary: A plain non-cuffed airway tube used in infants and young children where the circular cricoid cartilage forms a natural anatomical seal.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Clear curved plastic tube with centimetre depth graduations and a standard 15 mm machine connector.
Lacks an inflatable cuff, inflation line, and pilot balloon.
Distal tip has a smooth rounded bevel.

blocks.title: Anatomical rationale
bullets: In children under 8 years of age, the narrowest point of the airway is the complete rigid circular ring of the cricoid cartilage.
The funnel-shaped subglottic airway forms a snug natural seal around an uncuffed tube.
Maximizes internal lumen diameter to minimize work of breathing in small airways.

blocks.title: Sizing formula
bullets: Cole formula for internal diameter: ID (mm) = (Age in years / 4) + 4.
Depth formula at lips: Depth (cm) = (Age in years / 2) + 12.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Avoids the hazard of cuff overinflation causing ischemic necrosis of delicate subglottic mucosa and subglottic stenosis.
An audible air leak should be present at 20 to 25 cmH2O to ensure the tube is not wedged too tightly in the cricoid ring.

viva.q: Why were uncuffed tubes traditionally preferred in children under 8 years?
viva.a: The circular cricoid cartilage is the narrowest point of the paediatric airway, forming a physiological anatomical seal without a cuff.

viva.q: What formula calculates the internal diameter of an uncuffed tube in a child?
viva.a: Cole formula: Age in years divided by 4, plus 4 mm.

viva.q: What complication is avoided by not using high cuff pressure in children?
viva.a: Subglottic mucosal ischemic necrosis, which can result in life-threatening acquired subglottic stenosis.

image.brief: Paediatric uncuffed endotracheal tube showing centimetre markings, smooth beveled tip without a cuff, and standard 15 mm hub.

items.summary: A three-part silver or stainless steel tracheostomy assembly with a removable inner cannula designed for long-term airway maintenance.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Highly polished silver or stainless steel curved metallic tube.
Composed of 3 distinct matching parts: outer cannula with neck flange, inner removable cannula with swivel latch, and solid pilot introducer.
Outer cannula remains in the trachea; inner cannula slides inside and locks; pilot obturator blunts the tip during insertion.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Long-term or permanent tracheostomy maintenance.
Bilateral vocal cord paralysis and chronic upper airway obstruction.
Post-laryngectomy breathing stoma.
Home tracheostomy care in tracheostomized patients.

blocks.title: Advantages
bullets: Silver is non-irritating to mucosa and possesses natural bactericidal oligodynamic properties.
Inner cannula can be unlocked, cleaned of crusted secretions, boiled or sterilised, and replaced without decannulating the patient.
Durable and lasts for years with simple home cleaning.

blocks.title: Disadvantages
bullets: Uncuffed: cannot protect against aspiration of gastric contents or pharyngeal secretions.
Lacks a standard 15 mm connector, making connection to positive-pressure mechanical ventilators difficult.

viva.q: What are the three components of a Chevalier Jackson tracheostomy tube?
viva.a: The outer cannula with neck flange, the inner removable cannula with locking latch, and the blunt pilot (obturator).

viva.q: What is the crucial clinical advantage of the inner removable cannula?
viva.a: If dried mucus or sputum crusts obstruct the lumen, the inner cannula can be withdrawn and cleaned while the outer tube holds the airway open.

viva.q: Why is the Chevalier Jackson tube unsuitable for mechanical ventilation?
viva.a: It is an uncuffed metal tube lacking an airtight seal and standard 15 mm ventilator connector, allowing positive-pressure gas to leak.

image.brief: Chevalier Jackson silver metallic tracheostomy tube disassembled showing outer cannula, inner cannula, and blunt pilot introducer.

items.summary: A thermosensitive PVC tracheostomy tube with a low-pressure cuff and 15 mm machine connector designed for prolonged mechanical ventilation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: White or clear curved thermosensitive PVC tube with a soft swivel neck flange.
Equipped with a standard 15 mm swivel machine connector for ventilator tubing.
Features a fine pilot inflation line with a spring valve and a distal low-pressure high-volume cuff.
Supplied with a blunt introducer stylet.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Prolonged mechanical ventilation in ICU patients (expected ventilation beyond 10 to 14 days).
Protecting the lungs against massive aspiration in comatose or head-injured patients.
Facilitating pulmonary toilet and tracheobronchial suctioning in respiratory failure.
Weaning patients from mechanical ventilation.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Tracheo-innominate artery fistula if tube is sited too low (below 4th tracheal ring) and erodes into the brachiocephalic artery.
Tracheoesophageal fistula from excessive cuff pressure eroding the posterior membranous tracheal wall.
Tracheal stenosis at the cuff site; tube blockage by dried secretions.

viva.q: When is a patient switched from an endotracheal tube to a tracheostomy tube in ICU?
viva.a: When mechanical ventilation is anticipated to exceed 10 to 14 days, to prevent laryngeal ulceration and reduce airway resistance.

viva.q: What catastrophic vascular complication can occur if a tracheostomy is sited too low?
viva.a: Tracheo-innominate artery fistula, where the cuff or tip erodes the innominate artery, resulting in fatal exsanguinating hemorrhage.

viva.q: What is the rationale for using thermosensitive PVC in Portex tubes?
viva.a: It softens at body temperature, conforming to the patient tracheal anatomy to reduce mucosal pressure points.

image.brief: Curved white Portex tracheostomy tube with neck flange, blue pilot balloon, and inflated transparent tracheal cuff.

items.summary: A multi-lumen radiopaque polyurethane catheter inserted into the superior vena cava via internal jugular or subclavian vein using the Seldinger technique.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long flexible polyurethane catheter with centimetre depth graduations along the shaft.
Splits at the proximal end into 3 labeled colour-coded extension tubes with pinch clamps and luer locks.
Lumens: Distal port (16G brown), Medial port (18G blue), Proximal port (18G white).
Supplied in a sterile kit with introducer needle, J-tip guidewire, scalpel, and vessel dilator.

blocks.title: Uses of specific lumens
bullets: Distal port (16G brown): exits at the catheter tip; used for central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring and viscous blood infusions.
Medial port (18G blue): dedicated to total parenteral nutrition (TPN) infusions to reduce line contamination.
Proximal port (18G white): used for routine intravenous medications, inotropes, and blood sampling.

blocks.title: Seldinger technique
bullets: Puncture vein with introducer needle; confirm non-pulsatile dark venous blood return.
Pass J-tip guidewire through needle into vein; withdraw needle leaving wire in place.
Make small skin nick with scalpel; advance vessel dilator over wire into vein; withdraw dilator.
Thread catheter over guidewire until the tip exits the distal hub; grasp wire tip firmly and advance catheter into vein.
Remove guidewire; verify blood return and flush all three ports with heparinized saline; suture catheter wings to skin.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Pneumothorax and haemothorax (more common with subclavian approach).
Accidental arterial puncture (carotid or subclavian artery haematoma).
Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI).
Air embolism and cardiac arrhythmias from guidewire irritation of right atrium.

viva.q: What is the Seldinger technique in central venous catheterisation?
viva.a: A percutaneous method: needle puncture, guidewire insertion, needle removal, tract dilation over the wire, catheter threading, and wire removal.

viva.q: Name the three lumens of a standard central line and their primary uses.
viva.a: Distal 16G for CVP monitoring and viscous fluids, medial 18G for parenteral nutrition, proximal 18G for drugs and blood sampling.

viva.q: What mandatory investigation follows internal jugular or subclavian line insertion?
viva.a: An upright chest radiograph to rule out pneumothorax and verify the tip lies in the lower superior vena cava above the pericardial reflection.

image.brief: Triple-lumen central venous catheter kit displaying flexible catheter, three-port manifold, J-tip guidewire, dilator, and introducer needle.

items.summary: An over-the-needle PTFE catheter with a metal stylet, flashback chamber, and colour-coded gauge system for intravenous access.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Plastic catheter sheath mounted snugly over an inner bevelled stainless steel needle stylet.
Transparent flashback chamber at the base of the stylet.
Top port with colour-coded injection cap and flexible side fixation wings.
Universal colour-coded gauge system stamped on wings and packaging.

blocks.title: Standard colour codes and flow rates
bullets: 14G (Orange): 240 mL/min; massive trauma resuscitation and rapid blood transfusion.
16G (Grey): 180 mL/min; major surgical operations and fluid resuscitation.
18G (Green): 90 mL/min; standard blood transfusion and routine surgery.
20G (Pink): 60 mL/min; maintenance intravenous fluids and drug administration.
22G (Blue): 36 mL/min; elderly patients and fragile veins.
24G (Yellow): 20 mL/min; paediatric and neonatal peripheral access.

blocks.title: Poiseuille law and flow mechanics
bullets: Flow rate is directly proportional to the fourth power of the internal radius and inversely proportional to catheter length.
A short, large-bore peripheral cannula (14G or 16G) delivers fluid significantly faster than a long central venous line.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Superficial thrombophlebitis, cannula-site infection, extravasation with subcutaneous infiltration, and hematoma.

viva.q: Which colour IV cannula is selected for rapid blood resuscitation in hemorrhagic shock?
viva.a: Orange (14G) or Grey (16G), because their large internal diameter provides the highest volumetric fluid delivery rates.

viva.q: What physical principle explains why a short 14G cannula infuses faster than a central line?
viva.a: Poiseuille law: flow rate is proportional to the fourth power of the radius and inversely proportional to catheter length.

viva.q: What does blood appearing in the flashback chamber indicate?
viva.a: It confirms that the tip of the stainless steel needle stylet has penetrated the lumen of the vein.

image.brief: Array of peripheral intravenous cannulas arranged side by side showing standard colour codes: orange 14G, grey 16G, green 18G, pink 20G, and blue 22G.

items.summary: A calibrated balloon catheter designed to be passed beyond arterial emboli, inflated with saline, and withdrawn to sweep out occluding clots.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Slender, flexible radiopaque catheter marked with centimetre graduations along the shaft.
Features a colour-coded hub indicating French size (2 Fr to 7 Fr).
Distal tip has a soft rounded tip and a miniature inflatable latex or polyurethane balloon.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Emergency surgical thromboembolectomy for acute lower or upper limb arterial ischemia.
Extracting thrombus from thrombosed hemodialysis arteriovenous fistulas or synthetic vascular grafts.
Biliary stone extraction during open common bile duct exploration.

blocks.title: Steps of operation
bullets: Test balloon integrity and determine inflation volume with sterile saline before insertion.
Perform transverse arteriotomy (e.g., common femoral artery).
Pass deflated catheter gently through arteriotomy past the occluding thrombus.
Inflate balloon with precise volume of sterile saline until mild resistance is felt.
Gently withdraw catheter under steady tactile tension, sweeping the embolus out through the arteriotomy.

blocks.title: Complications and precautions
bullets: Arterial rupture or intimal dissection from overinflating the balloon or pulling with excessive force.
Always inflate with liquid (saline), never air: liquid is non-compressible and provides immediate tactile resistance feedback to the surgeon.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical indication for a Fogarty catheter?
viva.a: Emergency arterial embolectomy to extract an occluding embolus and restore limb perfusion in acute limb ischemia.

viva.q: Why must a Fogarty balloon be inflated with liquid rather than air?
viva.a: Liquid is non-compressible, transmitting instant tactile resistance feedback to the surgeon hand to prevent arterial over-distension.

viva.q: What catastrophic arterial complication can occur from overzealous balloon traction?
viva.a: Intimal flap dissection, arterial wall rupture, or complete avulsion of the vessel.

image.brief: Calibrated Fogarty embolectomy catheter showing the miniature distended balloon at the tip and colour-coded French hub.
